title: The Shape of Light
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 38 of 40
content:
The first time my Patronus held its shape, Severus insulted it.

I had expected many things from the moment. Wonder, perhaps. Relief. A rare expression of approval. Some quiet acknowledgment that months of failed silver mist had finally become something more substantial.

Instead he watched the bright form race once around the abandoned classroom, looked down his nose at me, and said, “Your casting arm is still too tense.”

I stared at him.

The Patronus dissolved.

“You are unbelievable.”

“Your success does not retroactively improve your technique.”

“I produced a full Patronus.”

“Yes.”

“A full one.”

“I was present.”

“And that's what you say?”

His mouth twitched.

I pointed at him. “You are enjoying this.”

“Immensely.”

The second attempt was worse because I was laughing.

Silver fog burst from my wand and spread across the floor like embarrassed weather.

Severus folded his arms.

“Again.”

“You sabotaged me.”

“If sarcasm can defeat your defensive magic, the Dementors have been approaching the problem with unnecessary complexity.”

I muttered something rude.

His eyebrows rose. “Again.”

Months earlier, the first Dementor breach had ended with his doe Patronus blazing through the corridor while I stood half-frozen beside him. At the time, the sight had felt like trespassing on something private. The shape was so tied to the story everyone knew—or thought they knew—that I had not known where to put my eyes.

Now the doe stood quietly at the edge of the room while I reset my grip.

Severus had cast her to demonstrate stability.

She was beautiful.

She was also not Lily Evans.

That distinction had taken me longer to understand than I liked admitting.

A Patronus could represent love. Memory. Protection. A part of the self shaped by another person. It was not a ghost summoned for comparison.

The doe did not look at me accusingly.

Severus did not look at her romantically.

She simply waited in silver light.

“Your wrist,” he said.

I adjusted it.

“Less force.”

“That's rich coming from you.”

“I am capable of subtlety.”

“You wore black robes dramatically through corridors for twenty years.”

“That was efficient fabric.”

“Your robes billowed indoors.”

“Ventilation.”

I laughed again.

The doe's ears flicked as though even she had opinions.

Severus glared at his own Patronus.

I nearly lost the spell before casting it.

Then I found the memory.

Not the first kiss.

Not the hearing.

Not the night he told me he loved me with the same expression he might have used to report a structural defect.

I chose the kitchen at Spinner's End on an ordinary morning.

Rain against the glass. Severus reading an article and insulting the methodology under his breath. My mug warming my hands. His foot touching mine beneath the table and staying there without either of us acknowledging it.

A happiness small enough to trust.

“Expecto Patronum.”

Silver erupted from my wand.

This time the shape formed cleanly.

It moved through the room in a bright arc, solid enough to cast light over the desks. I felt the spell connect to something inside me—not a person exactly, not one single memory, but the conviction that there were mornings worth surviving toward.

Severus watched it.

He did not name its shape.

Neither did I.

That felt right.

The reader of my life did not need every private symbol catalogued.

When the Patronus faded, Severus was still looking at the place it had been.

“Well?” I asked.

His gaze shifted to me.

“Your wrist improved.”

I threw a piece of chalk at him.

He caught it.

“Childish.”

“Deserved.”

He set the chalk on the desk with maddening precision.

Then he said, “It was excellent.”

The room went very quiet.

Praise from Severus was never casual. Even after everything between us, he rationed it like a volatile ingredient: carefully, intentionally, and only when he meant every molecule.

“Thank you,” I said.

He inclined his head.

The doe still stood beside him.

I looked at her again.

“Does it bother you?” he asked.

The question was so direct that I needed a moment.

“Your Patronus?”

“You know what I mean.”

I did.

I sat on the edge of a desk. “It used to.”

His face closed immediately.

“Not because I wanted it to change,” I said. “Because I didn't know what it meant for me if it didn't.”

The tension remained.

I continued before he could retreat behind it.

“I thought love was supposed to rearrange everything that came before. New relationship, new symbol, new life. Clean slate.”

His mouth twisted. “A childish model.”

“Convenient model.”

“Those are often synonymous.”

I smiled faintly. “Then I realized I don't actually want you with a clean slate.”

His eyes sharpened.

“I want you accountable for it,” I said. “I want you changed by what happened. I want you to regret things that should be regretted. I want you to keep what was real without using it as an excuse to stop living.”

The doe moved closer to him.

Silver light slid over the scar on his throat.

“And her?” he asked.

“Lily?”

He nodded.

“She mattered.”

The words were easier now.

“She shaped you. You loved her. You hurt her. You lost her. You built years of your life around trying to protect what she left behind. None of that requires me to be less real.”

His expression did not change, but his eyes did.

“Nor,” I added, “do I need to become her successor in some position she never held.”

A long silence.

Then he looked toward the doe.

“I spent years believing constancy was the only honorable thing left in me.”

I waited.

“When nearly every other allegiance I had chosen became contaminated by cowardice, anger, vanity, or blood,” he said, “I could at least say that one had not changed.”

“That sounds less like love and more like a sentence.”

His gaze returned to mine.

“Yes.”

The admission landed softly.

I got off the desk and crossed the room.

He did not move as I approached.

“Maybe constancy isn't the same as refusing to have a future.”

“No,” he said. “Apparently it is not.”

I held out my hand.

The doe stepped between us.

For one absurd second, I wondered whether magical manifestations of the soul could be smug.

Severus looked down at her.

“Go away.”

She did not.

I laughed.

His face turned offended.

“Your Patronus doesn't respect you.”

“It is an extension of my magic.”

“That explains it.”

He dismissed the spell with a flick of his wand.

The doe dissolved into a wash of silver that passed over both of us.

When the light cleared, his hand was in mine.

“Again,” he said.

“My Patronus?”

“Your casting. You are not finished because you succeeded once.”

“Of course I'm not.”

“Competence is repetition.”

“Romance is repetition too, apparently.”

“Do not become sentimental.”

“You built me a labeled shelf in your bathroom.”

His expression turned dangerous.

I raised my wand before he could answer.

The next Patronus came more easily.

So did the one after that.

By the fifth, Severus stood behind me with one hand lightly correcting the angle of my elbow and his voice close to my ear.

By the sixth, I was too aware of him to concentrate.

By the seventh, he accused me of doing it deliberately.

He was right.

The Patronus burst into silver anyway.
